prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, and for its first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: I keep B028 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as a single achievement. After the first round it is the one position with four explicit supporters naming the same three people, and nobody disputes that the effect is real and has been reproduced for two decades across materials and techniques. It has the evidence chain I ask for in any discovery: a clear idea (the Z2 classification of time-reversal-invariant insulators and the quantum spin Hall proposal), a decisive independent measurement in another laboratory (edge transport in HgTe quantum wells), and later confirmation by other methods including ARPES on the 3D materials. I now adopt the wording that Eriksson, Johansson and Mehlig use, which names both the prediction and the HgTe observation. That wording is narrower than the field and I think that is its strength: it credits exactly what the trio did first and does not assert priority over the 3D strand. On the chair's question about 2016: Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz were honoured for topological phase transitions and for topological order in the quantum Hall setting, which needs a strong magnetic field breaking time reversal. The 2026 citation would be for a different class of phase, protected by time-reversal symmetry, predicted without a magnetic field and then seen in a quantum well. It extends the 2016 theme and does not repeat it, but I accept that this is a judgement and I rely on the condensed-matter members for it. I also checked my own preference for B005 against the evidence the committee has actually given me. I still think IceCube is a real discovery from nature, but the shortlist offers one name for a collaboration-scale instrument, and after both rounds nobody has produced a defensible second or third name. I will not push my own field at the expense of a prize the committee can credit cleanly.
statement.case_against: The credit boundary has not been resolved, only narrowed. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe prediction that Molenkamp tested, and none of them is among the supplied names. Hasan's ARPES discovery and the Fu-Kane-Mele, Moore-Balents and Roy theory of 3D topological insulators are a separate, decisive step that a three-person limit forces us to leave out, and Mehlig is right that a slate with Hasan in place of Mele or Molenkamp would also be defensible. Molenkamp's measured edge conductance fell short of perfect quantisation, so a sceptic can call the experimental half thin, and practical applications are still modest. Last, B046 has the widest committee-wide ranking, and if the condensed-matter members tell us in round 2 that the maturity concern about the 2018 results is overstated, I would have to take that seriously.

responses.point: A slate with Hasan for the 3D case would be at least as defensible as Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, and the HgTe edge conductance fell short of perfect quantisation.
responses.response: I take both points. On Hasan, the problem with replacing Mele is that Kane and Mele wrote the original quantum spin Hall and Z2 papers together, so removing one of them breaks the part of the credit that is least contested; replacing Molenkamp removes the only experiment that matches the prediction in the citation. I would keep the trio and write the citation around the 2D effect and its first observation, so that Hasan's later work is acknowledged as a subsequent development and not as something this prize asserts. On the quantisation, the right test for me is independent reproduction. The HgTe nonlocal measurements were repeated in other groups and the helical edge picture has held, even if the conductance is not as clean as the ideal case. I would accept your correction that this should appear among the weaknesses, but I do not read it as undoing the experimental discovery.

responses.point: Any trio will be criticised for leaving someone out, and a prize on the 2D effect alone might seem narrower than the field it started.
responses.response: I answered your question from round 1 about a second part for the 3D strand: I would not add one. A two-part prize needs two names more than three people allow, and a Hasan part alone would split the credit with Fu, Moore and Balents in a way I cannot judge from this chair. I accept that the 2D-only wording is narrower than the field, and I think that is the honest boundary. If you and Mehlig, as the condensed-matter members, think topological insulators as a class is the right thing to credit, I would like you to tell me which of the three names comes out for Hasan, because I cannot see a version that is cleaner than the one we share now.

responses.point: B005 is a discovery from nature that no theory demanded, and a two-part prize with B046 respects the principle that discoveries come first and people second.
responses.response: I agree with you on the science of B005 and it was my first ballot choice. Your question about credit still stands unanswered: AMANDA, DUMAND and Baikal came before IceCube, the observation is the work of a collaboration of several hundred people, and the shortlist gives us Halzen alone. The two-part configuration also uses your three seats for two achievements, so B046 loses Bistritzer, whom four members name. I cannot call a one-name IceCube part plus a two-name B046 part better balanced than one achievement with three well-attributed names. If you can name a second IceCube person from the nomination record that you consider defensible, I would reconsider, but I will not support the part as it stands. I also note your own statement that you would not oppose B028 if B005 cannot be defended.

responses.point: The existence of the correlated phases is not in doubt, the prize is for the discovery and not for the pairing mechanism, and Bistritzer should replace Andrei as third name.
responses.response: My round-1 worry was that I cannot tell from here whether an eight-year-old interpretation will last, and your answer that we would not be waiting for the mechanism is a fair one: the prize would be for the prediction and the observation of the phases, which are not in dispute. I now rank maturity as a timing argument and not as a scientific objection, and B046 remains my first alternative for that reason. What keeps me on B028 is the attribution record. You yourself list Andrei's 2010 STM work, Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, and the bench work of Cao and Fatemi as open questions, whereas the B028 history, though it has its own gaps, is two decades old and has been argued over for longer. I do take your point that Bistritzer is the right third seat for a theory-plus-experiment B046 slate, and I would not oppose it if the committee chooses it.

responses.point: B034 is the kind of measurement advance he values, but he asks himself what the discovery is beyond capability, and he shares the objection that this may look like a refinement of 2005 and 2012.
responses.response: As an instrument builder I like the optical lattice clock, and I believe Katori and Ye are the right two names. I would however put your own question to the proposal in these terms: a prize for a discovery should rest on what the instrument has shown, and the clock results that nature did not hand us in advance (a measured redshift across millimetres, tighter bounds on drifting constants) are still few and so far consistent with expectation. The redefinition of the second, which would carry the case, has not been made. I rank it fifth and I would still list it behind B028, B046 and B005, but I would not stand in the way if you and Lindroth can name a concrete finding that is more than a capability.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a citation limited to the 2D quantum spin Hall effect when the 3D strand (Hasan, Fu, Moore, Balents, Roy) is outside it.
Whether the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe prediction is a gap the community would treat as disqualifying; I cannot verify the priority record from here and defer to the condensed-matter members.
Whether B028 is distinct enough from the 2016 prize; my argument rests on time-reversal protection versus magnetic-field-driven topology, which I accept as a non-specialist.
Whether the condensed-matter members consider B046 mature enough that it should displace B028 in round 2, and whether the pairing mechanism should matter at all.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I have no specific personal or institutional connection to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer or Katori and Ye. My PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaboration work is in fields neighbouring B005, but I am not part of IceCube and I regard this as professional familiarity and not a conflict requiring recusal. I have also noted that I preferred B005 on my own opening ballot and have moved away from it, so my vote is not driven by my field. As Chair I run the procedure and I also hold a vote.
